props.title: The Gleaners and I
props.initialSlug: A poetic journey through France's modern scavengers

sections.content: The Gleaners and I (2000) revolutionized personal documentary filmmaking through Agnès Varda's intimate exploration of modern-day gleaners in France. Using a small digital camera, Varda follows people who collect leftover crops, urban discards, and forgotten objects - while reflecting on her own role as a gleaner of images. The film connects directly to Jean-François Millet's famous 1857 painting "The Gleaners," but pushes far beyond simple documentation. Varda's approach influenced later works like Stories We Tell (2012) and The Act of Killing (2012), showing how deeply personal filmmaking can illuminate broader social issues.

sections.content: Varda's innovative use of consumer-grade digital cameras in The Gleaners and I marked a crucial shift in documentary aesthetics. The lightweight equipment allowed for intimate moments that would have been impossible with traditional film crews. This approach influenced later works like Cameraperson (2016) and Honeyland (2019), where the boundary between filmmaker and subject becomes deliberately blurred. The handheld camera becomes both tool and character, with Varda frequently filming her own hands and reflecting on aging through the lens. SUBHEAD: Social Commentary Through Personal Lens

The film's examination of waste, poverty, and sustainable living remains startlingly relevant. Varda's empathetic portraits of gleaners - from rural potato pickers to urban dumpster divers - anticipated later documentaries about food waste like Just Eat It (2014) and Wasted! The Story of Food Waste (2017). But where those films take broader institutional approaches, Varda keeps her focus intimate and personal, showing how individual stories illuminate systemic issues.
